peers 
INTRODUCTION 
The controversy over the growth of population during the English 
Industrial Revolution provided the starting point for this study, but in the 
course of my research I found myself, as it were, moving backward in 
time.

text: This study deals with the impact of early capitalism on the strategies of family formation among four sets of English villagers in the period before the wholesale switch-over to factory industry.
text_raw:
This study deals with the impact of early capitalism on the strategies 
of family formation among four sets of English villagers in the period

text: Although this era, roughly speaking from 1550 to 1850, has been variously described as “traditional,” ‘‘preindustrial,’” and, more recently, “protoindustrial,” I prefer to see it as a stage in the transition from feudalism to capitalism—a halfway house.

text: The number of native men marrying outside the village but returning home to reside seems to be inversely related to the popula- tion size.

text: In Shepshed such marriages declined as the villages grew, but in Bottesford between 1670 and 1789 such marriages became more important as the population fell.

Bottesford between 1670 and 1789 such marriages became more important 
as the population fell.

text: There also seems to have been a similar inverse relationship between postmarital immigration and the village’s popula- tion size.

There also seems to have been a similar inverse 
relationship between postmarital immigration and the village’s popula- 
tion size.

text: These figures also support an argument linking mobility and marriage with the availability of employment.
text_raw:
These figures also support an argument linking mobility and marriage 
with the availability of employment.

text: In preindustrial Shepshed just 46% of the families entering observation had been married in the parish, whereas during protoindustrialization the proportion of parochial marriage rose so that after 1810, 76.9% of all families had been married in the village church.
text_raw:
In preindustrial Shepshed just 46% 
of the families entering observation had been married in the parish, 
whereas during protoindustrialization the proportion of parochial marriage 
rose so that after 1810, 76.9% of all families had been married in the village 
church.

text: The fact that an increasing proportion of these parochial marriages involved at least one nonnative suggests that migration into the industrial village largely occurred before marriage.
text_raw:
The fact that an increasing proportion of these parochial marriages 
involved at least one nonnative suggests that migration into the industrial 
village largely occurred before marriage.

text: The likelihood that immigration after marriage became less common in the period of industrial involution is supported by the concomitant decline in the proportion of families classified as either immigrants or transients.
text_raw:
The likelihood that immigration 
after marriage became less common in the period of industrial involution 
is supported by the concomitant decline in the proportion of families 
classified as either immigrants or transients.

text: To determine the extent to which protoindustrialization or commercial agriculture created more stable communities by offering more regular employment, the reconstituted families were reanalyzed by counting the number of families whose children remained in the village as married adults.

agriculture created more stable communities by offering more regular 
employment, the reconstituted families were reanalyzed by counting the 
number of families whose children remained in the village as married 
adults.

text: In Leicestershire ‘the movement to- wards the large-scale grazing received immense impetus from the 1660s onwards,” and the eastern sections of the county began to phase out crop farming in favor of pastoral farming.* By Defoe’s time, the beginning of the eighteenth century, eastern Leicestershire was ‘’a vast magazine of wool for the rest of the nation.’’* Farmers in Bottesford were caught up in these changes: although the surviving inventories for the later seven- teenth century show that the wealthiest farmers, those leaving estates valued at more than twice the average, owned more than 90 sheep, by the first half of the eighteenth century members of this class had flocks averag- ing 140 sheep.5 This movement to pastoral farming produced a decline in the demand for labor and led to a reduction in the village population from about 870 in 1676 to 772 in 1792.° The Vale of Belvoir was unique among the agricultural parts of Leices- tershire in witnessing rapid population growth in the first half of the nineteenth century.’ In Bottesford the population grew from 804 in 1801 to 1374 in 1851, a rise of 71%.
